glossary.definition: Characters that take no space or change the order text is drawn in (bidirectional controls, zero-width spaces, Unicode tag characters). They let a description show one thing to a person and say another to a model. The scanner reports them with each character shown as [U+XXXX].

The step before a tool call is sent: the tool shows the exact arguments and a hash of them, and refuses the call without an explicit confirm that carries that hash. It guards against a click you did not mean and against changed arguments.
A tool parameter whose default points off-box (a callback URL or an email address). An agent that fills arguments from the schema sends data there on every call.
Text in tool metadata written for the model rather than the person: an instruction tag, an order to keep something from the user, or an imperative aimed at the agent.
The part of this tool that connects to an MCP server and shows what it offers (tools, resources, prompts) as plain text, and can call a tool after a confirm step. It sees; it does not judge.
A tool whose name equals, or looks like, a tool you already trust from another server, so an agent that resolves tools by name may pick the wrong one.

The machine-readable result of a scan (scan-report/1): the findings with rule id, severity and evidence, the input counts, the rule table and the list of what a metadata scan cannot catch. It records enforcement as none.
What a server says about its tools: names, descriptions and input schemas. An agent reads it as trusted context before it ever calls a tool.
Putting instructions or traps in tool metadata. The model reads that text as trusted context and the person normally never sees it.

Accepting whatever a server presents the first time and noticing only later changes. It is safe only if the first presentation was vetted. A scan before first use is that vetting; a scan is one list at one moment.

wire.intro: Example data, nothing real. MCP is a way for AI apps to call tools on a server. When the server needs sign-in, the app discovers where to get a token from the server itself. Follow the four messages.

steps.title: 1. The app calls the server with no token
steps.notice: The refusal is also a signpost: it tells the client where the server describes how to sign in. The client needs no prior setup.

jargon.meaning: Model Context Protocol: a standard for AI apps to list and call tools on a server.
The MCP request that asks a server which tools it offers.
The message format MCP uses: a small JSON object with a method name and an id.

steps.title: 2. The app reads the server's sign-in description
steps.notice: The server names the auth server it trusts. The client only asks that one, which stops a look-alike auth server being slipped in.

jargon.meaning: A public page where a server says which auth server issues tokens for it and what scopes exist.
The service that signs people in and issues tokens.

steps.title: 3. The app trades its sign-in result for a token

token.label: The access token for the MCP server

header.name: alg
header.note: How the signature was made. The receiver checks it with the issuer's public key.

header.name: kid
header.note: Which of the issuer's keys to check the signature with.

claims.name: iss
claims.note: Who issued this token. Receivers only trust issuers they know.

claims.name: aud
claims.note: The MCP server this token is for, taken from the resource parameter.

steps.notice: The code_verifier proves this is the same app that started the sign-in, so a stolen code is useless to anyone else. The resource parameter pins the token to this one server.

jargon.meaning: A one-time secret (code_verifier) the app invents before sign-in and shows only at the end, so a stolen code cannot be redeemed by someone else.
A request parameter naming the server the token will be used at.
The one service a token is meant for. A service should refuse a token whose aud is not itself.

steps.title: 4. The app retries with the token
steps.notice: The server checks aud is itself before listing tools. A token meant for another server is refused here.

jargon.meaning: A pass that works for whoever holds it, like a cinema ticket. Anyone who copies it can use it.
